After Hours: The Sixth Tab
Six tabs. Five people swear they paid. The rain isn't stopping.
Six friends get stuck in a flooding bar after last call. Soon nobody cares who paid — only who stays to carry the boxes.

It's Friday after last call at the Halfmoon, the storm has shut down the buses, and the closeout shows one tab nobody will claim. Then the basement floods, the power dies, and six friends — plus one exhausted temp manager — have to decide who carries what, whose stories get recorded, and who gets to go home. Mason and Ethan are still not talking about the knee, the bench, and who told the coach. You decide how Nico runs the night: by asking, not by promising for everyone.
The temp manager covering the Halfmoon's night shift — the one with the keys, the mop, and no dinner since noon.
If nobody owns the work, the bar floods, a stranger's kindness goes to waste, and six friends leave owing each other something they can't name.

The Sixth Tab
Square the tabs — and get everyone home safe
The Halfmoon, main bar
Friday, 11:52 PM
Last call was twenty minutes ago. Rain hammers the front window. The temp manager prints the closeout and slides it down the bar to Nico.
I read it twice. I read it upside down. The math doesn't care how I hold it.
Six tabs. Five people claiming they paid.
Sounds like a wedding.
Sounds like you.
I paid! I have a receipt. Somewhere. Spiritually. And Theo doesn't even run tabs.
Cash only. I like to feel the money leave.
Outside, a bus rolls past without stopping — OUT OF SERVICE. Mason checks his phone. Ethan is already zipping his jacket, pointedly not looking at him.
Somebody has to decide what happens first. Apparently that's me, because I'm the one who said one more round.
What does Nico sort out first?
Count the tabs now. Then sort rides.
I read the tabs aloud like roll call. Mason, paid. Ethan, paid. Wren, Rowan, paid. Mine — paid, thank you. Tab six: no name, already closed.
Closed by who?
Nobody knows. Then every ride app flashes the same thing: surge pricing, forty-minute waits, flood advisory. Nobody's going anywhere tonight.
Nico read every tab aloud: all five were paid and tab six was closed with no name, before a flood advisory kept everyone in.
Rides first. The tabs can wait.
Tabs later. Who's got a safe way home? Hands.
Me. I can get home alone.
I open my mouth. I close it. He said alone.
Then the city sends a flood alert to every phone at once. Buses suspended. Nico folds the printout into his pocket, unsolved.
Nico put rides ahead of the tabs; Ethan said he'd get home alone, a flood alert stranded everyone, and the tab mystery stayed in Nico's pocket.
Not your tab. Hand it to the manager.
I slide the printout back across the bar. I'm a customer with good comedic timing, not the accountant.
Respectfully, this is above my pay grade, which is zero.
Fine. Then you don't get to joke about it later.
The manager pockets it. A minute later, the flood alert hits every phone, and the manager looks at the six of them like someone doing new math.
Nico handed the tab problem to the manager and declined to run the count; the flood alert trapped them all anyway.
Nobody Just Has Opinions
Everyone agrees to one real job
The basement stairs
Saturday, 12:31 AM
The basement door is open. Water laps the third step. The manager calls up the stairs: kegs, paper goods, everything on the floor comes up. Now.
Paper first, it dies fastest. Kegs take two people. Nobody touches the outlet by the freezer.
I can lift the mood.
I hand him a case of tonic water. Twenty-four cans. Heavy on purpose.
Try the box.
Ethan bends for the nearest keg. Before he can tip it, Mason is on the other end. Neither says a word. They haven't since Tuesday.
I'll narrate. Somebody should document this.
Somebody should carry this. Both hands, Wren.
Six people, one staircase, nobody allowed to just have opinions. That includes the guy who suggested one more round.
How does Nico split the work?
Everyone names one job. Out loud.
Roll call, part two. Say your job so we can hold you to it. I'm on mop.
Theo: boxes. Wren: paper goods, both hands. Rowan: the line on the stairs. Mason and Ethan, without looking at each other: kegs.
At 12:58 the last keg clears the top step. The lights flicker once — and die. In the dark, a small red light blinks on.
Nobody move. Six people, one storm, no power. Everyone tells one true story before the lights come back. I'm rolling.
Everyone named one job out loud — Nico took the mop — and all the stock came up before the power went out.
Dry goods only. Kegs wait for daylight.
Paper and boxes. The kegs stay. That water's too close to the outlet.
I already have my hands on the rim. Ethan says, 'We said no.' I let go.
Twenty minutes later the shelves upstairs are full of napkins, and the kegs sit in dark water below. Then the lights die. A small red light blinks on.
Okay. Nobody move. No power, no exits, six of us. One true story each before the lights come back. I'm rolling.
Nico limited the job to dry goods and left the kegs below for safety; Mason let go of the keg when Ethan said no.
Call the owner. You're customers, not crew.
I stay at the top of the stairs and call the owner. Voicemail. I call again. My phone's flashlight is the most useful thing I do all night.
Look at you. Lighting design.
The other five carry everything anyway, one tired trip at a time. Then the power cuts out for real. In the dark, a small red light blinks on.
Nobody move. No power, no exits. Six people, one true story each, before the lights come back. I'm rolling.
Nico refused to haul stock and tried the owner instead; the other five carried everything up before the power failed.
Recording in the Dark
Check recording consent, person by person
The main bar, by candlelight
Saturday, 1:40 AM
Six candles from the storage closet. Forty minutes of stories. Theo's worst audition. Rowan's cousin's wedding. Ethan, quietly: the knee, the bench, and who told the coach.
I stare at the candle while he says it. I told the coach. I'd do it again. I'd also ask first. Both are true.
I watch the little red light on Wren's recorder. It's been on the whole time.
Wren. Did you ask them?
I was going to ask everyone after—
I hear it as I say it. I set the recorder on the bar like it's hot.
I asked after. That's not the same.
Now you know.
Ethan's story is on that thing. So is mine. The room is waiting for someone to say what happens to it.
What happens to Wren's recording?
Keep only what each person signs off on.
Go around. Each of us says yes or no to our own part. No reasons required.
Theo: yes, it's my best material. Rowan: yes. Nico: yes, unflattering edit welcome. Mason: no. Ethan: no.
I delete Mason's clip and Ethan's clip while they watch the screen. Nobody has to explain anything.
Thanks.
Each person approved or refused their own clip; Wren deleted Mason's and Ethan's in front of them and kept only what was cleared.
Stop recording. Everyone grabs a mop.
Off. Nobody reviews anything tonight. We clean.
I press stop and zip the recorder into my bag. Forty minutes, sealed, nobody's yes or no on file yet.
That's unfinished.
That's unfinished with a mop in its hand. We sort the file in daylight.
Recording stopped and nothing was published; the file stayed sealed in Wren's bag with consent still unresolved.
Post the storm story now. Ask later.
It's gold, Wren. Post a teaser. We'll sort permissions when the power's back.
I hesitate exactly long enough to feel like a coward, then post forty seconds. Ethan's voice is in it.
Wren pulls it twelve minutes later. Too late: Ethan's phone lights up — a teammate, three question marks. He moves to the stool by the door.
You didn't ask.
At Nico's urging, Wren posted a forty-second teaser without asking; it included Ethan's story, and a teammate heard it before she pulled it.
Who's Still on the Clock
Every job agreed to by its owner — and leaving isn't a crime
The whiteboard behind the bar
Saturday, 2:45 AM
I wipe the specials off the whiteboard and draw six empty boxes. No names. I hand out markers like ballots.
Pick one you can finish.
I volunteer for morale.
Morale has a mop.
I can label the stock. No microphone.
I will count the tabs.
I take this end if Ethan wants the other.
Ethan looks at the marker, then at Mason, for a long second. One box is still empty, and the manager, asleep on their feet, is watching it.
How does Nico run the board?
Everyone writes their own. Leaving counts too.
I add one line under the boxes: LEAVING IS ALLOWED. TEXT WHEN HOME. Nobody's a villain for wanting a bed.
I write KEGS — W/ MASON. My handwriting is worse than my mood. Mason doesn't smile. Mostly doesn't.
Under MORALE I write MOP, in capitals, and initial it like a contract.
Each person wrote their own job; Ethan chose kegs with Mason, Theo signed up for the mop, and Nico added that leaving was allowed.
Split shifts. Half work, half rest.
Forty-five on, forty-five off. Nobody gets heroic. Heroic people faint.
Mason lands on first shift. Ethan on second. Mason opens his mouth to trade. Ethan shakes his head once.
I'm good with second.
Rowan set 45-minute shifts; Mason and Ethan ended up on different shifts, and Ethan declined to trade.
Hand Rowan the marker. You're not the boss.
I'm counting tabs, not people. Rowan, you're the board.
Fine. Then I set an end time: five a.m. After that I stop, and nobody guilts me.
The boxes fill slower without Nico talking everyone into them. Theo writes his name in the last box himself. Nobody asked him to.
Nico refused to run the board and handed it to Rowan, who set a hard 5 a.m. end time; Theo filled the last empty box on his own.
What Sixty-Four Dollars Buys
Accept that one kind meal can't fix everything
Behind the register, by flashlight
Saturday, 4:10 AM
I finally find it in the register log. Tab six. Opened 8:14 PM by a stranger at the window seat. Paid in full: sixty-four dollars.
There's a note. 'For whoever's stuck working tonight. Eat something.'
Every head turns to the manager, who hasn't eaten since noon and is currently holding a wet mop.
The basement pump is nineteen hundred, minimum. The floor's a separate problem.
So we weren't the heroes.
We can still mop.
That's the episode title.
It's not an episode. It's a floor.
Sixty-four dollars, one meal, one stranger. It was never supposed to save the place. It was supposed to feed one person.
What does the group do with what's left?
Feed the manager. Then mop until it's dry.
I fire up the flat-top by flashlight and make the manager the worst grilled cheese in the city. Paid for. Tab six, closed properly.
Then six people mop in a line, back to front, until the floorboards stop squelching at 5:20.
Done.
Nico cooked the prepaid meal for the manager, and all six mopped the floor dry by 5:20 AM.
Pass a jar. Anonymous, any amount.
I set an empty pickle jar on the bar. No names, no amounts, no speeches. Fold it, drop it, walk away.
By five, the jar holds two hundred and eleven dollars and one IOU in Theo's handwriting. Not nineteen hundred. Not nothing.
I'll email the owner the total. Just the total.
The group pooled $211 anonymously in a jar toward the pump repair; nobody was told who gave what.
Call it. Anyone who wants to go, goes.
Rain's easing. Anybody who wants to go home, go. Nobody's keeping score.
Rowan leaves at five exactly, as promised, and texts from the car. Wren follows. Theo keeps mopping, humming a show tune nobody asked for.
I stay too. Not for credit. The tabs still don't make sense, and the manager still hasn't eaten.
Nico called the night; Rowan and Wren went home and texted when safe, while Theo and Nico stayed to keep cleaning.
Breakfast, Not Directions
Ask before offering company
The Halfmoon, front windows
Saturday, 6:05 AM
Grey light. The rain has stopped like it's embarrassed. Mason comes out of the kitchen with two plates of eggs and sets one at Ethan's stool.
Eat. Or don't.
There's a napkin under the plate with three bus routes written on it. None of them circled.
You looked up my bus.
Looked up three. Didn't pick.
Ethan eats half the eggs. Mason wipes the same clean glass for a full minute. Then he puts it down.
Want company?
Until the bus. Then we'll see.
The rest of us are very busy stacking chairs. Extremely busy. Professionally not listening.
What does Nico do with the room?
Clear the room. Give them the door.
Everybody to the back. These chairs won't stack themselves, and Theo's form is terrible.
Mason and Ethan walk out into the wet morning. At the stop, Ethan turns to him before the bus pulls in.
Next time, ask me before the coach. Not after.
Okay. Before.
Nico cleared the room; Mason walked Ethan to the bus, Ethan asked to be told first next time, and Mason agreed.
Walk everyone to the bus stop together.
Group walk. Fresh air, sore backs, nobody alone on a wet sidewalk.
Six people and a manager straggle down the block. Theo narrates the puddles. Mason and Ethan walk at the back — close, but not alone.
At the stop, I bump his shoulder with mine. That's all. It's not nothing.
The whole group walked to the bus stop together; Mason and Ethan didn't get time alone, but Ethan bumped Mason's shoulder before boarding.
Back Ethan's call: he can go alone.
He said he can get home. That's his call, not ours.
I almost say until the bus. Then I don't. I take the eggs in a to-go box and go alone, because I can.
I nod. I wash both plates. I wash them very hard.
Nico backed Ethan's choice to go alone; Ethan left by himself with the eggs, and Mason let him go without following.
Next Time Isn't an Accident
Confirm the group lunch and any private invite — separately
The Halfmoon, reopened for one hour
Saturday, 10:30 PM
The owner reopens for one hour so the six can return the spare keys and collect their jackets. The floor smells like bleach and good intentions.
I hold up my phone. The group chat is called THE SIXTH TAB now. I did not name it. I'd like credit anyway.
Sunday lunch. Here. One table. No flood.
And an end time.
You wound my spontaneity.
I am not recording that.
Ethan, want company on the bus?
Ask me Sunday. Tonight I am going home.
Two invitations on the table. One for everyone, one for one person. They shouldn't have to share an answer.
How does Nico send the invite?
Send it: one to three. Ask each person.
I send it. Sunday, 1 to 3 PM. No boxes. Reply yes or no — both count. Five yeses come back before I pocket the phone.
Sunday, then.
Sunday. Ask me then. I'll have an answer.
Nico sent a Sunday lunch invite from 1 to 3 and five people said yes; Ethan told Mason to ask him again on Sunday.
Keep it loose: optional, no RSVPs.
Lunch is happening. Come if you want. Nobody's taking attendance. Especially not Rowan.
I'm taking attendance silently.
Nobody commits. Everybody saves the address. Mason doesn't ask Ethan again; he just holds the door, and Ethan says thanks.
Nico made lunch optional with no RSVPs; nobody committed, and Mason didn't press his invitation to Ethan.
Skip lunch. Say a real goodbye tonight.
Actually — tonight was enough. Let's not make it a franchise. Say your thank-yous, go home.
They do it standing up. Theo thanks the mop. Wren thanks the people who said no. Ethan thanks the manager, and nobody else in particular.
I don't ask about the bus again. He said tonight he's going home. I heard him.
Nico called off the lunch; the group said goodbye that night, and Mason didn't repeat his invitation to Ethan.
Six Coasters
Choose how — and whether — to work together again
The Halfmoon, the long table
Sunday, 1:05 PM
Sunday. The pump is fixed with the owner's grudging credit card and whatever the six of them chipped in. Six coasters wait on the long table, no names.
I put my recorder on the table, face up, file list open so everyone can see what's left. Nothing from anyone who said no.
We end at three. I mean it. I'm gone at 3:01.
I brought a mop. As a joke. Mostly as a joke.
I come in last. Mason stands up like he's about to make a speech, then just doesn't. Good.
You can ask now.
Six coasters. Nobody's here by accident anymore. The question is what we do with that.
What does Nico ask the table to choose?
Six coasters. Everyone signs their own.
I pass the marker. Each person signs one coaster and writes one thing they'll show up for. The manager tacks all six above the bar.
Want company? After lunch. The whole way.
Yes. The whole way.
Six chairs. Nobody's here by accident.
Everyone signed a coaster for something they'd show up for; Ethan said yes to Mason's company the whole way home.
Keep the schedule. Skip the speeches.
No speeches. Rowan's got a sheet: who helps which Saturday. Sign up or don't.
Four names go on the sheet. Lunch ends at 2:58. Nobody hugs. Everybody says see you.
Ask me again in a few weeks, Mason. I'm not saying no.
Same time next flood. With an end time.
The group kept a volunteer schedule without getting closer; Ethan asked Mason to ask him again in a few weeks.
End it. Delete the tape. Leave the door open.
We used things that weren't ours, and some of us skipped the work. Me included. So this ends today.
I delete the storm file in front of everyone — teaser, backups, all of it — and turn the screen so they can watch it go.
Deleted. All of it. Watch me.
Thanks. Ask me again in a month. I might say yes.
Nico ended the gatherings, owning that the group misused private stories; Wren deleted every unauthorized recording, and Ethan left the door open for later.
Six Chairs
The work got split by consent, the tape kept only yeses, and six signed coasters hang over the bar. Mason walks Ethan home the whole way, because Ethan said yes.
Six chairs. Nobody's here by accident.
Same Time Next Flood
The pump is fixed, the schedule holds, and nobody pretends they're closer than they are. Mason waits to be asked again; Ethan means it when he says he isn't saying no.
Same time next flood. With an end time.
Deleted
The group ends honestly: the private stories are deleted where everyone can watch, and nobody is forced to stay friends. Trust is broken, not burned — Ethan leaves the door open a crack.
Ask me again in a month. I might say yes.
Six Ways Home

Tab six on the register, two people carrying one keg, the empty bar at dawn.
Six voice notes, each recorded and approved by its speaker. Nothing private gets stitched in.
